OK, I missed that you already mentioned in your first message Thunderbird not responding. Now please try to start Thunderbird in "troubleshoot mode" : hold down the Shift key while launching Thunderbird. https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/troubleshoot-mode-thunderbird If Thunderbird still doesn't respond, force-quit the application:

Now try to open the Thunderbird profile folder: press the Windows key and start typing %APPDATA%\Thunderbird\Profiles\ This will open the folder "Profiles" in the Windows file explorer. "Profiles" may contain one or several folders: if you see only one folder "xxxxxxxx.default", open it, look for the prefs.js file and retrieve its size. If the size is 6 to 7 kB it happens to be a newly created file which doesn't contain any account settings , and you will have to look for a prefs-1.js (or invalidprefs.js) file with a much bigger size and an actual time stamp. This prefs-1.js (or more general prefs-x.js) file would be the corrupt "old" prefs.js file which has be renamed in prefs-1.js by Thunderbird.

If you see more than one folder in "Profiles", such as xxxxxxxx.default and yyyyyyyy.default-release (or ......default-esr) , then open the ...default-release or the default -esr folder and search for the prefs.js and a prefs-1.js files

content:
Those verification codes (known as "two-factor authentication) are sent by the system you are trying to use - they have nothing to do with Thunderbird, per se, except that often the code is being emailed to you, and if you want to read the email in Thunderbird, Thunderbird must have permission to access the email account where the code is being sent. If you're waiting for a code from that email provider, but Thunderbird is not yet authorized to access that account, you can't retieve that email. Workarounds could include...

- Use your email provider's web mail to read the email with the code;

- Have the code sent to an alternate email address (you usually have to have verified this alternate with them in advance so they know for sure that it's really you;)

- Have the code sent to a different mobile phone (you usually have to have verified this alternate with them in advance so they know for sure that it's really you. In your case, maybe you could have the code sent to your daughter and she can read it to you over the phone - she doesn't necessarily need to be there in person;)

- Some hosts have the option of makeing a voice call to you, and they will read the code to you.

- Call your email host and ask their advice on the best way to get the code to you.

content:
Thunderbird works very well with Comcast - I use it daily and have for years. And though I have always used IMAP, I haven't heard anything about them discontinuing POP3 access, and I doubt they would (but nothing's impossible.)

This page has their recommended settings. How do they compare with yours?

https://www.xfinity.com/support/articles/email-client-programs-with-xfinity-email

One thing that's not addressed there is that, sometime in the past year or so, they appear to have implemented OAuth2 as an available authentication method, and that's what I've been using lately. But I'm pretty sure they still accept the old, less-secure Normal Password method.

Here are my working Comcast settings (with OAuth2 authentication.) I have no way to test the POP3 settings, but I think they should work.)

IMAP (Incoming): Incoming Server Type: IMAP Mail Server Incoming Server Name: imap.comcast.net Port: 993 User Name: <my email address> Connection Security: SSL/TLS Authentication method: Normal Password OR OAuth2

POP3 (Incoming): Incoming Server Type: POP Mail Server Incoming Server Name: pop3.comcast.net Port: 995 User Name: <my email address> Connection Security: SSL/TLS Authentication method: Normal Password (or OAuth2?)

SMTP (Outgoing): SMTP Server Name: smtp.comcast.net Port: 465 Connection Security: SSL/TLS Authentication method: Normal Password OR OAuth2 User Name: <my email address>

Before you start messing around with server settings, especially if you have been using POP3, which means your archived messages exits ONLY on you local computer, I recommend that you make a safety backup of your entire Thunderbird Profile. If your saved messages are precious, you should consider doing this regularly.

Here's an article about how to find and backup your Profile. I recommend using the manual method, and avoid Thunderbird's Export tool.

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/profiles-where-thunderbird-stores-user-data#w_backing-up-a-profile

Let's check what exists in profile - share images so we are on same page as you.

  • Exit Thunderbird
  • Access profile name folder
  • click on 'Mail' folder
  • click on pop mail account name folder

You should have an mbox file (no extension) and a .msf file of same name for the renamed main folder. As I do not know the name of the renamed main folder, let's pretend it's now called 'Hobbies'.
